Herman Hollerith's Tabulating Machine
sources.license: Smithsonian terms of use; facts only

facts.text: The United States takes a census of its whole population every ten years (the decennial census).
Census results are used to divide seats in Congress among the states; officials feared the 1890 count would not be finished by 1900, which would have made this impossible.
The 1880 census was tabulated with a tally-sheet machine that could not keep up with the data; final tabulations were not finished until 1887.
Tabulating the 1880 census took about 7 years (almost a decade by another Census Bureau page).
Experts estimated that without new machines the 1890 census would have taken 13 years to tabulate.
Herman Hollerith was born in Buffalo, New York, in 1860, earned a mining engineering degree from Columbia in 1879, and worked on the 1880 census.
In the early 1880s, while riding a train, Hollerith noticed the conductor's punched tickets, which helped inspire his approach.
Hollerith first tried rolls of paper with holes, then chose cards because they lasted longer and fed through a counter more easily.
Each card stood for one person, and each hole position stood for one characteristic; for example, one position meant male and another meant female.
In the reader, metal pins passed through the holes into cups of mercury; each completed electric circuit moved forward the dial for that characteristic.
The 1890 tabulators had 40 counting dials; clerks punched about 500 cards a day each, and an experienced clerk could process 80 cards a minute.
In 1888 the census office held a contest for a faster method, using 1880 census data from four areas of St. Louis; three contestants took part.
In the contest, preparing the data for counting took the two rivals 44.5 and 55.5 hours and took Hollerith 5.5 hours; capturing the data took them 144.5 and 100.5 hours and him 72.5 hours.
Derived: Hollerith's 5.5 hours of preparation was less than one-eighth of the faster rival's 44.5 hours and about one-tenth of the slower rival's 55.5 hours.
Hollerith won the contract to process and tabulate the 1890 census; his patent for electrical tabulation was granted on 8 January 1889.
The 1890 census was the first to use Hollerith's electric tabulating system; information from the forms was punched onto cards that were run through the machines.
The census office leased a fleet of Hollerith machines, and the 1890 count finished months ahead of schedule and far under budget.
In 1890 clerks tabulated data for nearly 63 million people, and the results were published 18 months sooner than those of the 1880 census.
Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896.
For the 1900 census Hollerith raised his rental prices to a level the government found intolerable, so the Census Bureau began building its own machines.
In 1911 Hollerith's company and three others formed the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, which was renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.
Modified versions of Hollerith's machines stayed in use at the Census Bureau until electronic computers replaced them in the 1950s; UNIVAC I was installed in 1951.

notes: 1880 年普查的統計時間各來源說法不一（美國普查局一頁寫到 1887 年才完成最後的統計、約 7 年；另一頁寫將近十年；任務提示的「將近 8 年」找不到白名單來源），選文以「到 1887 年才完成、約七年」為準。
